emocore.d: The first emo wave inside hardcore: lyrics turn from slogans to confession, dynamic swells replace the straight-ahead charge, and Washington, DC is the starting point.

midwest-emo.d: Second-generation emo: hardcore's intensity folded into slow, off-kilter guitar conversations; college-town basements and American Football's self-titled album are the watershed.

emo-pop.d: Emo's confessionals stuffed into pop-punk's big choruses, the mainstream sound of 2000s MTV and the Warped Tour.

emo-revival.d: The fourth emo wave of the 2010s underground: math-rock guitars plus more direct self-dissection; the Modern Baseball generation brought it back to small rooms.

screamo.d: Emo and hardcore pushed to extremes: screaming, fractured structures and explosive dynamics; the 90s San Diego and French scenes each formed their own camp.

math-rock.d: Built on rhythmic games: odd time signatures, constant metre shifts and tapped guitar turn rock into precision gears; Slint's Spiderland set the template and Japan's toe made it lighter.

mathcore.d: Math rock's rhythms plus metalcore's weight and screaming; Dillinger Escape Plan turned it into pure adrenaline.

grindcore.d: Punk and death metal crossbred at top speed: songs lasting seconds, blast beats and political fury; Napalm Death's Scum defined the word.

crust-punk.d: Hardcore plus metal plus anarchism: raw, low and apocalyptic; Amebix and Doom are the source.

d-beat.d: The one-beat-one-hit drum pattern Discharge invented, copied by countless bands into a subgenre: fast, thick wall of sound, vocals like shouted orders.

street-punk.d: The street lineage of Oi! and punk: football-terrace singalongs and working-class narratives, UK in the 80s.

oi.d: The street branch of British punk after 1977; slogan choruses tangled up with skinhead culture, simple and direct, written for the terraces.

ska-punk.d: Ska's jumping rhythms plus punk's speed and distortion; the core of the US third wave in the late 80s.

anarcho-punk.d: The UK anarcho-punk sparked by Crass: anti-war, anti-consumerism, DIY labels and collage visuals, more a way of organising than a music.

riot-grrrl.d: The women-led punk movement of the 90s, which wrote gender politics into distortion and zine culture.

horror-punk.d: Punk with B-movie horror aesthetics; the Misfits' monster imagery and melodic choruses defined the style.

psychobilly.d: Rockabilly's slapback bass plus punk's speed and horror-film imagination; The Cramps are the true ancestor.

nwobhm.d: The New Wave of British Heavy Metal: Iron Maiden and Saxon brought punk's speed and twin-guitar melodies into metal, the starting point of metal's 1980s global spread.

speed-metal.d: A faster, meaner transitional form beyond traditional heavy metal; Motörhead's drive is the prototype, leading straight to thrash.

crossover-thrash.d: Hardcore punk and thrash crossing over; Suicidal Tendencies' Institutionalized is the definitive template for the fusion.

doom-metal.d: The slow heavy music Black Sabbath started: downtuned, crushing and apocalyptic; it later split into sludge, funeral doom and drone.

sludge-metal.d: Doom's slowness plus hardcore's filth; New Orleans' Eyehategod and Crowbar turned it to mud, and Mastodon made it clearer in the 2000s.

stoner-rock.d: Slowed down, downtuned and distortion wide open, with a whole set of desert and psychedelic imagery; Kyuss and Sleep are holy ground.

desert-rock.d: The stoner offshoot of the California desert scene; Queens of the Stone Age took it into the mainstream.

power-metal.d: European melodic metal: high-speed double kick, clean high vocals and fantasy-epic themes; Helloween fixed the form.

symphonic-metal.d: Metal bands with orchestras and choirs; Nightwish brought operatic female vocals into metal and Within Temptation took the more pop path.

gothic-metal.d: Goth rock's cold gloom plus doom's weight; Type O Negative and Paradise Lost represent two routes.

industrial-metal.d: Industrial samples meeting metal riffs; Ministry's Psalm 69 is the peak, and Nine Inch Nails made it more personal.

folk-metal.d: Folk melodies and traditional instruments enter metal; Skyclad broke the ground and Finntroll danced humppa into metal.

viking-metal.d: Norse myth mixed with black metal and folk; Bathory's Hammerheart set the paradigm and Amon Amarth turned it into war songs.

melodic-death.d: Death metal's blast beats plus twin-guitar melody; the Gothenburg sound shaped metalcore through the whole 2000s.

tech-death.d: Death metal made technical: complex time signatures, atonal solos and extreme difficulty; Death's Symbolic is the dividing line.

brutal-death.d: The heaviest branch of death metal: guttural growls, top-speed blast beats and gore themes; Suffocation and Cannibal Corpse are representative.

deathcore.d: Metalcore plus death metal: breakdowns alternating with blast beats; it moved from the US underground into the mainstream in the late 2000s.

djent.d: Meshuggah-style syncopated low-end riffs with clean tones and precise production; the Periphery generation turned it into a genre name.

post-metal.d: Post-rock's long build-ups plus sludge's weight; Neurosis and Isis made metal into slowly shifting terrain.

blackgaze.d: Black metal's tremolo and shoegaze's foggy harmonies converge; Alcest and Deafheaven made it the most visible metal offshoot of the 2010s.

funeral-doom.d: The extremely slow version of doom: a twenty-minute song, pipe organ and funeral atmosphere; Skepticism and Thergothon are the source.

drone-metal.d: Metal that stretches one chord to its limit: walls of sound, feedback and space; Earth and Sunn O))) made it a physical experience.

goregrind.d: The bloody variant of grindcore and death metal; Carcass's early work defined its tone, themes and pathological cover art.

war-metal.d: Black metal at its most primitive and violent: raw recordings, war themes and almost no melody; Blasphemy is the origin point.

dsbm.d: A slow, shrieking, minimally repetitive branch of black metal; Burzum and Xasthur represent two temperaments: solitude and self-consumption.
